title: Python Strings and String Literals
learningObjectives: Explain the core rules of python strings and string literals in Python.
Write valid Python syntax for the operations covered in this topic.
Predict results for ordinary inputs and relevant edge cases.
Identify immutability, return values and error behaviour where applicable.
Apply the topic to a realistic text-processing task.

understand.concept: A string is an immutable sequence of Unicode code points used to represent text. String literals are written with matching single or double quotes; triple quotes allow a literal to span multiple lines. Python has no separate character type: indexing a string produces another string, even when it contains one character.
understand.whyItMatters: Text appears in names, messages, identifiers, reports, user input and data files. Knowing how strings are represented helps prevent accidental mutation assumptions and encoding mistakes.
understand.analogy: A string is like a printed label: you can read it and make a revised label, but you do not alter the original printed characters in place.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not describe Unicode representation, object identity or the fact that a new string may share implementation-level storage. A Python str represents Unicode text, not a raw byte array.

explain.narrative:
## String values and literals
A `str` value represents Unicode text. Put matching single quotes or double quotes around a literal. Choose the delimiter that makes embedded quotation marks readable, or escape a delimiter when necessary. Triple single or double quotes preserve line breaks and are also commonly used for docstrings.

## Immutability and character access
Strings are immutable: operations such as replacement create a new string rather than changing the existing object. Python does not have a distinct `char` type. A one-character selection is still a `str`. Indexing is zero-based, and an index outside the valid range raises `IndexError`.

## Unicode and practical choices
A visible symbol can consist of more than one Unicode code point, so a string index is not always the same as a user-perceived grapheme. Use `len()` for the number of code points in the string. Convert bytes explicitly when working with encoded data.

questions.prompt: Which built-in type represents Python text?
questions.explanation: Python text is represented by the immutable str type; bytes is a separate type for byte sequences.

questions.prompt: Which literal can span several source-code lines directly?
questions.explanation: Triple single or double quotes allow literal line breaks within the quoted text.
Indexing a string returns a one-character string; Python has no separate char type.

questions.prompt: What happens when code tries to assign to text[0]?
options: A new string is silently returned
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable, so item assignment is not supported.
The string contains six Unicode code points, so len returns 6.
